It's just about how you define 'British.' Just because it was older doesn't mean it was boring.

Vikings basically started attacking 'us' (I am from the British Isles) from just before 800AD. We would say that 'us' at this time were the Anglo-Saxons, who had already driven the Celtic inhabitants (now known as Welsh and Cornish) west and south. They started by raiding, but then they kind of stayed.

Through the century they established a kingdom that is roughly what is north and east of a line between a major northern city and the capital.

So a lot of modern-day 'British' have Viking ancestry, especially in the old Viking kingdom (that came to be known as the Danelaw). So Vikings did a mixture of two things- settle and farm, and raid and attack. Sometimes they received national "protection money" for not doing the attack and raid bit- this ransom was called Danegeld.

Under a notable Anglo-Saxon king, the Anglo-Saxons got their act together, beat the Vikings, gained symbolic overlordship over them, and the two parts of England kind of lived in peace for a bit. There was a very famous ruler of the Viking territory called Eric the Bloodaxe.

Gradually the Anglo-Saxon territory got stronger and between about 950 and about 1010 it was all ruled by the Anglo-Saxons.

Then, because the Anglo-Saxon territory got weaker, partly because of a king known for his poor advice, for most of the period 1013-1042 the Danes ruled all of England, and their most famous king was Canute.

Then the Anglo-Saxons returned, and in 1066, for complex (but interesting) reasons, the Vikings tried invading from the North and completely independently, the Normans (who were originally Vikings that had settled in northern France) invaded from the south.

King Harold beat the Vikings in the North, marched his men back down but lost to the Normans at Hastings in 1066 and that's where, traditionally, English history starts.

Well - ELI5 is:

FPTP- one who gets most votes wins. Each race is separate, like a horse or athletics race.

Proportional Representation- it's like a cake. More votes= bigger slice of the cake. BUT, your vote is not just for one person, it's for a pool of people / a party- a lot of "races" are lumped together in the cake and so there are lots of winners.

There are LOTS of different systems of PR, from where you have 2nd, 3rd preferences and so on if your top choice is 'knocked out' to a straight system where you vote for no individual, just a party.

People dislike FPTP because you can get loads of votes for a party nationally but very few representatives, and vice versa, just with a relatively small % of the vote you can get lots of representatives. If you live in a safe district, it's like your vote is 'wasted.'

People dislike PR because the connection between your vote and the PERSON you vote for to represent you is weaker. And because it HAS to be more complicated than FPTP. As we've seen specifically when people have been giving tribute to a notable local representative, but also when representatives are discussed in general, they are important local figures who help their constituents with individual problems, not just members of a party nationally.

When there was a referendum (!) recently about whether to change FPTP to PR, FPTP won. Few actually were bothered to vote though.

Usenet and seedboxes are different things.

Downloading from Usenet uses your own bandwidth.

Seedboxes are parts of servers located elsewhere in the world, separate from your own computer. They have their own connections and their own bandwidth. Their allowance is typically much higher than what an average person would ever need, so it's often marketed as 'unlimited.'

When you transfer files between the seedbox and your own machine, you do use your bandwidth. However, if you are torrenting from your seedbox, that does not consume any of the bandwidth from your own connection.

For instance, if you were using a seedbox to improve your ratio on private trackers, the upload you receive from those torrents would not count against your home bandwidth, since it is being handled by a server located elsewhere.
